ofdm-mimo-001.question: Why can an OFDM transmitter modulate many subcarriers all at once with an IFFT (inverse fast Fourier transform), without an oscillator for each subcarrier?
choices: Because the IFFT lowers the peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) of the transmitted signal, so the waveform is not distorted in the amplifier even when many subcarriers are superposed
Because with the subcarrier spacing equal to the reciprocal of the useful symbol duration, the OFDM samples are exactly the inverse DFT of the data on the subcarriers
Because the IFFT itself acts as a filter that removes multipath delayed waves, so neither a cyclic prefix nor per-subcarrier equalization at the receiver is needed any more
ofdm-mimo-001.explanation: Let the N subcarrier frequencies be k/Tu (Tu is the useful symbol duration), put data Xk on each, and add them up. Sampling this signal at intervals of Tu/N gives x(n) = Σ Xk e^(j2πkn/N), which has the same form as an N-point inverse discrete Fourier transform. So the IFFT computation alone modulates all subcarriers, and the receiver can separate them in one go with an FFT. The IFFT does not lower PAPR; OFDM, in which many subcarriers overlap, is in fact a scheme with a large PAPR. Countering delayed waves is the job of the cyclic prefix and per-subcarrier equalization; the IFFT itself does not remove delayed waves.

ofdm-mimo-002.question: An OFDM signal is generated with a sampling frequency of 30.72 MHz and a 2048-point FFT. What is the subcarrier spacing?
choices: 15 kHz
7.5 kHz
30 kHz
ofdm-mimo-002.explanation: An N-point FFT handles the frequency components that divide the sampling frequency fs into N equal parts, so the subcarrier spacing is Δf = fs/N = 30.72×10⁶ Hz / 2048 = 15 kHz. The useful symbol duration is its reciprocal, Tu = 1/Δf ≈ 66.7 µs, which matches exactly the length of N samples (2048 × (1/30.72 MHz)). 7.5 kHz is the mistake of treating the band as extending only up to fs/2, as for a real-valued signal, and dividing that into N parts; 30 kHz is the mistake of counting the 2048 points as real I and Q samples together and dividing by 1024 complex samples. N subcarriers are lined up including the negative-frequency components; in practice both ends are left empty as guard bands, so fewer than N subcarriers are used.

ofdm-mimo-003.question: Which statement about the effect of adding a cyclic prefix (CP) in front of each OFDM symbol is correct?
choices: The CP removes the phase jump at symbol boundaries, which also cancels the carrier frequency offset between transmitter and receiver, so frequency offset correction becomes unnecessary
The CP repeats the whole symbol once more, and adding the two copies at the receiver raises the received S/N by 3 dB without increasing the transmit power

If the CP is longer than the channel's delay spread, the channel convolution becomes circular over the FFT window, so each subcarrier can be corrected with a single complex multiplication (one-tap equalization)
ofdm-mimo-003.explanation: The CP is a copy of the end portion of the symbol attached to its front. If the spread of the delayed waves is shorter than the CP, the delayed waves of the previous symbol fall within the CP interval and are discarded, and over the interval taken into the FFT the signal looks as if it continues periodically. The linear convolution then becomes identical to a circular convolution, and after the FFT each subcarrier is simply multiplied by H(k), so it can be equalized by dividing by a single complex number. Frequency offset is a separate problem that breaks orthogonality, and the CP cannot correct it. The energy in the CP interval is discarded rather than used for demodulation, so the S/N and efficiency actually fall by that amount.

ofdm-mimo-004.question: When the OFDM CP (cyclic prefix) is 4.7 µs long, which is closest to the upper limit of the path-length difference from the direct wave of a delayed wave that can be absorbed without intersymbol interference? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
choices: About 1.4 km
About 0.7 km
About 20 km
ofdm-mimo-004.explanation: If a delayed wave arrives within the CP length, the components of the previous symbol stay within the CP interval. The upper limit of the delay is 4.7 µs, so the path-length difference can be up to 4.7×10⁻⁶ s × 3×10⁸ m/s = 1410 m, about 1.4 km. About 0.7 km is the mistake of dividing by 2 as if it were a round trip, like radar range. On a propagation path the wave travels only one way, so you do not divide by 2. About 20 km is the value obtained using the useful symbol duration (about 66.7 µs) instead of the CP. In environments where waves reflect off mountains or large buildings and take detours of several km, a longer CP is needed.

ofdm-mimo-005.question: A CP of length 0.8 µs is added to an OFDM symbol whose useful symbol duration is 3.2 µs. What fraction of the total time is occupied by the useful symbol that carries data?
ofdm-mimo-005.explanation: The length of one symbol is 3.2 + 0.8 = 4.0 µs, of which 3.2 µs carries data, so the fraction is 3.2/4.0 = 0.8, or 80%. The transmission rate becomes 0.8 times that without a CP, and the S/N loss from discarding the power in the CP interval at the receiver is 10 log₁₀(4.0/3.2) ≈ 0.97 dB. 75% is the mistake of 1 − 0.8/3.2, subtracting the CP length as a ratio to the useful symbol duration; the denominator must be the total length. 20% is the fraction of the total taken by the CP (the overhead), the opposite of the fraction of the useful symbol asked for. A longer CP gives more tolerance to delay, but this overhead grows.

ofdm-mimo-006.question: Without changing the bandwidth, the number of OFDM subcarriers is increased and their spacing narrowed. Which is correct as a general property (the CP length is unchanged)?
choices: The narrower the subcarrier spacing, the shorter the useful symbol duration, so the CP fraction rises, efficiency falls, and the system becomes weaker against delayed waves even with the same CP
More subcarriers carry more symbols at once while the symbol rate per subcarrier stays the same, so the transmission rate increases in proportion to the number of subcarriers
The useful symbol duration becomes longer and the CP fraction falls, raising efficiency, but the system becomes more vulnerable to intercarrier interference from Doppler and frequency offset
ofdm-mimo-006.explanation: Narrowing the subcarrier spacing Δf lengthens the useful symbol duration Tu = 1/Δf. With the same CP length, the CP's share of the total falls and efficiency rises; the maximum delay that can be absorbed is set by the CP length and does not change. On the other hand, Doppler frequency and frequency offset act as a ratio to Δf, so the narrower the spacing, the larger the intercarrier interference, and the longer symbol also adds processing delay. The symbol becomes longer, not shorter. With the same bandwidth, more subcarriers means a lower symbol rate per subcarrier, so the transmission rate stays almost the same; the only gain is the reduced CP overhead.

ofdm-mimo-007.question: In OFDM, pilots (known signals) for channel estimation are placed sparsely on the time–frequency grid. Which pair correctly gives the quantities that set the upper limit of the pilot spacing?
choices: The spacing in frequency is set by the coherence bandwidth (delay spread), and the spacing in time by the coherence time (Doppler frequency)
The spacing in frequency is set by the coherence time (Doppler frequency), and the spacing in time is set by the coherence bandwidth (delay spread)
Regardless of the propagation path, one pilot per symbol is enough to estimate the channel correctly on all subcarriers by interpolating in frequency
ofdm-mimo-007.explanation: The channel measured at the pilot positions is interpolated to get the values for the subcarriers and times in between, so the pilots must be dense enough to capture the channel's variation in a way that satisfies the sampling theorem. How fast the channel varies in frequency is set by the delay spread, and the pilot spacing in frequency is made sufficiently narrower than the reciprocal of the maximum delay (a measure of the coherence bandwidth). How fast it varies in time is set by the maximum Doppler frequency, and the spacing in time is made shorter than the coherence time. The pair with these two swapped is wrong. With one pilot per symbol, the variation of a frequency-selective channel cannot be interpolated. Denser pilots give more accurate estimates but leave fewer resources for data.

ofdm-mimo-008.question: In a MIMO system with 4 transmit antennas and 2 receive antennas, what is the maximum number of independent data streams that spatial multiplexing can send on the same frequency at the same time (assume the channel matrix has maximum rank)?
ofdm-mimo-008.explanation: The upper limit on the number of spatially multiplexed streams is the rank of the channel matrix H (2 receive rows × 4 transmit columns), and the rank cannot exceed the smaller of the rows and columns, min(4, 2) = 2. With only 2 receive antennas, the receiver gets only 2 independent observations, so it cannot separate 3 or more unknown data streams. 4 is the mistake of looking only at the number of transmit antennas; the remaining 2 antennas' worth of degrees of freedom is used as beamforming or transmit diversity gain. 8 is the number of transmit–receive antenna pairs (the number of matrix elements), not the number of streams. The capacity at high S/N also grows roughly in proportion to min(Nt, Nr).

ofdm-mimo-009.question: In a 2×2 MIMO system with a bandwidth of 20 MHz, two streams that do not interfere with each other are sent simultaneously, and each has a received S/N of 7 (linear). What is the total channel capacity by Shannon's formula?
choices: 60 Mb/s
240 Mb/s
120 Mb/s
ofdm-mimo-009.explanation: The two streams can be treated as parallel channels that do not interfere, so the capacity is the sum of the two. Per stream, C = B log₂(1 + S/N) = 20×10⁶ × log₂ 8 = 60 Mb/s, so the two together give 120 Mb/s. 60 Mb/s counts only one stream, corresponding to one antenna on each side. 240 Mb/s is the mistake of confusing the number of streams with the number of transmit–receive antenna pairs (2 × 2 = 4); the number of streams is min(2, 2) = 2. Even at the same S/N, spatial multiplexing has the advantage of multiplying capacity by the number of streams without increasing bandwidth.

ofdm-mimo-010.question: Which is correct about the properties of using the Alamouti code (a 2×1 space-time block code) with 2 transmit antennas and 1 receive antenna?
choices: Without channel knowledge at the transmitter it gives diversity order 2 at code rate 1, but at equal total power it is 3 dB worse than maximal ratio combining with 2 receive antennas
It is spatial multiplexing that sends different data from the 2 antennas, so even 1 receive antenna can separate the two streams and the transmission rate doubles
Power from the 2 transmit antennas combines, so compared with maximal ratio combining with 2 receive antennas it is 3 dB better at the same total transmit power, and the diversity order becomes 4
ofdm-mimo-010.explanation: In the Alamouti code, the two antennas send s1 and s2 at the first time instant and −s2* and s1* at the second. The receiver can separate the two symbols with simple linear processing, and the result combines the fading of both paths, so the diversity order is 2. Since 2 symbols are sent in 2 symbol times the rate is unchanged, and the transmitter needs no channel information. However, the total transmit power is split in half between the 2 antennas, so the average S/N is 3 dB lower than maximal ratio combining with 2 receive antennas. Saying it is 3 dB better is the reverse. It is a diversity scheme that sends the same data with coding, not spatial multiplexing that doubles the rate.

ofdm-mimo-011.question: A scheme that achieves the maximum diversity order of 4 is used with 2 transmit and 2 receive antennas. In the high-S/N region, if the average S/N is raised by 10 dB, by roughly what factor does the average bit error rate change (assume the error rate is proportional to S/N to the power −d, where d is the diversity order)?
ofdm-mimo-011.explanation: In the high-S/N region, the average error rate of a fading link is proportional to (S/N)⁻ᵈ. Raising the S/N by 10 dB (10 times) makes the error rate 10⁻⁴, that is, 1/10⁴ times. The diversity order is the number of paths that fade independently, and with 2 transmit and 2 receive antennas it is at most 2 × 2 = 4. 1/10 is the case of Rayleigh fading without diversity (d = 1), where raising the S/N by 10 dB lowers the error rate by only one order of magnitude. 1/10² is the mistake of counting only the number of transmit or receive antennas as the diversity order. The steeper slope of the error-rate curve is the effect of diversity.

ofdm-mimo-012.question: Which is correct about a 2×2 MIMO system in a strong line-of-sight environment, with the base station's 2 antennas placed close together?
choices: The higher the correlation between antennas, the more stable the phase relation of the two streams and the easier they are to separate, so the spatial multiplexing gain grows
Line-of-sight paths are stable, so the rank of the channel matrix is always the product of the numbers of transmit and receive antennas (4), allowing 4 streams
The channel-matrix columns become similar and the singular values spread apart (the condition number grows), so spatial multiplexing gain is hard to get, but beamforming power gain remains
ofdm-mimo-012.explanation: When the line-of-sight wave dominates and the antennas are closely spaced, the phase relationships of the paths from each transmit antenna to the receive antennas become almost the same, and the columns of the channel matrix become nearly parallel. The second singular value then becomes very small compared with the largest, and the second stream contributes almost nothing to capacity. Power can still be concentrated in the largest eigenmode, however, so beamforming gain remains. Saying that higher correlation makes separation easier is the reverse; spatial multiplexing suits propagation paths with low correlation and rich scattering. The rank never exceeds min(Nt, Nr) = 2, and it cannot be the product, 4.

ofdm-mimo-013.question: Which is correct about eigenmode transmission using the singular value decomposition H = UΣVᴴ when the transmitter knows the channel matrix H?
choices: Applying V at the transmitter and Uᴴ at the receiver gives interference-free parallel channels with the singular values as gains, and water-filling, giving more power to stronger channels, maximizes capacity
Giving more power to the weaker channels with smaller singular values so that all channels end up with exactly equal S/N maximizes the total capacity of the parallel channels
Regardless of the rank of H, the number of eigenmodes (parallel channels) is the sum of the numbers of transmit and receive antennas, so a 4×4 system has 8
ofdm-mimo-013.explanation: If the transmit vector is x = Vs and the received signal is multiplied by Uᴴ, then Uᴴy = Σs + Uᴴn, and since Σ is diagonal, each stream becomes an independent channel with gain equal to the singular value σi (the statistics of the noise Uᴴn are unchanged). The allocation that maximizes capacity under a fixed total power is given by the water-filling theorem: the lower a channel's "floor" (noise power divided by the power gain σi²), the more power is poured into it, and weak channels whose floor is above the water level get none. Concentrating power on weak channels to equalize S/N may make sense if the goal is equal error rates, but it lowers capacity. The number of parallel channels is the rank of H, which cannot exceed min(Nt, Nr).

ofdm-mimo-014.question: In eigenmode transmission, the values of "noise power / channel power gain" for two parallel channels are 1 and 3 (in the same units). When a total transmit power of 4 (same units) is allocated by the water-filling theorem, how much power goes to the second channel (the one whose value is 3)?
ofdm-mimo-014.explanation: In the water-filling theorem, the power for each channel is Pi = μ − Ni (Ni is noise power/gain, μ is the water level), and μ is chosen so that the total equals the total power. From (μ − 1) + (μ − 3) = 4, μ = 4, so 3 goes to the first channel and 1 to the second. The capacity is log₂(1 + 3/1) + log₂(1 + 1/3) ≈ 2 + 0.415 = 2.415 b/s/Hz. Splitting equally, 2 each, lowers it to about 2.32 b/s/Hz. Giving 3 is the reverse allocation that gives more to the weaker channel to make both S/N values equal to 1, and the capacity is only 2 b/s/Hz. If the total power is smaller and the water level falls below 3, the second channel gets no power at all.

ofdm-mimo-015.question: Which is correct about the linear detection methods used to receive spatial multiplexing, zero forcing (ZF) and MMSE (minimum mean square error)?
choices: ZF cancels interference and noise together with the inverse matrix, so it does not enhance noise; it has fewer errors than MMSE at any S/N, and the gap does not shrink even at high S/N
ZF removes interference completely but enhances noise on an ill-conditioned channel. MMSE minimizes the combined error from interference and noise, so it beats ZF at low S/N
MMSE removes inter-stream interference completely without regard to the noise level, but in exchange it greatly enhances noise, so it has more errors than ZF at low S/N, where noise dominates
ofdm-mimo-015.explanation: ZF multiplies the received signal by the (pseudo-)inverse of the channel matrix, making the interference between streams zero. But for channels with small singular values, the elements of the inverse become large and the noise is magnified by the same amount. MMSE uses weights that take the noise level into account, such as (HᴴH + σ²I)⁻¹Hᴴ, leaving a little interference in exchange for suppressing noise enhancement, and minimizes the mean square error. When the S/N is high enough, σ² becomes small and MMSE approaches ZF; at low S/N, MMSE is better. The statement that ZF does not enhance noise and the statement that MMSE removes interference completely both mix up the two properties.

ofdm-mimo-016.question: Which is the main reason the mobile uplink (terminal to base station) uses DFT-spread OFDM (SC-FDMA), in which data is spread by a DFT before being placed on the subcarriers, instead of ordinary OFDM?
choices: It widens the subcarrier spacing to improve Doppler tolerance, and the transmitted waveform's peak-to-average power ratio is the same as ordinary OFDM
The waveform becomes close to a single-carrier signal, lowering the peak-to-average power ratio so the terminal's power amplifier needs less backoff
It eliminates the need for a cyclic prefix, so the signal can be received without equalization even with delay spread, lightening the terminal's processing
ofdm-mimo-016.explanation: In ordinary OFDM many subcarriers add together, so the transmitted waveform's peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) is large, the power amplifier must be used with large backoff, and the loss of efficiency is a problem for battery-powered terminals. In DFT-spread OFDM, M data symbols are passed through a DFT, assigned to contiguous subcarriers, and returned to a time waveform by the IFFT, so the result resembles a filtered single-carrier signal and its PAPR is small. Adding a CP and equalizing in the frequency domain is the same as in ordinary OFDM; the CP is not eliminated. The subcarrier spacing can also be chosen the same as in ordinary OFDM, and improving Doppler tolerance is not the purpose.

ofdm-mimo-017.question: Which statement about OFDM leakage outside the band (out-of-band emission) is correct (assume each symbol is cut out with a rectangular time window)?
choices: Because the subcarriers are orthogonal, their spectral leakage outside the band also cancels, so no leakage occurs even when subcarriers are used right up to the band edges
Out-of-band leakage is set only by the length of the cyclic prefix, and the longer the CP the smaller the leakage, so windowing and filtering are unnecessary
Each subcarrier's spectrum is sinc-shaped with slowly decaying tails, so guard subcarriers are left empty at both edges and windowing or filtering suppresses the tails
ofdm-mimo-017.explanation: The spectrum of a subcarrier cut out with a rectangular time window has the sin(x)/x shape, whose amplitude falls only in inverse proportion to the frequency offset from the center, so its sidelobe tails extend a long way. Orthogonality means that the other subcarriers' components are zero at each subcarrier's center frequency; it does not mean the tails outside the band cancel. For this reason subcarriers at both edges of the used band are left empty as guards, and time windows that join symbol boundaries smoothly or transmit filters suppress the out-of-band emission. The CP length sets the tolerance to delayed paths and the symbol efficiency; it does not determine how the tails decay.

ofdm-mimo-018.question: An OFDM system has 100 data-carrying subcarriers, each modulated with QPSK (2 bits/symbol), with error correction at a code rate of 3/4. If the OFDM symbol length is 10 µs including the CP (useful symbol length 8 µs), what is the data rate?
choices: 15 Mb/s
20 Mb/s
About 18.8 Mb/s
ofdm-mimo-018.explanation: Each symbol carries 100 × 2 × 3/4 = 150 information bits, and the symbol period including the CP is 10 µs, so 150/(10×10⁻⁶) = 15×10⁶ b/s, 15 Mb/s. 20 Mb/s forgets to multiply by the code rate and includes the redundant error-correction bits. About 18.8 Mb/s divides by the useful symbol length of 8 µs excluding the CP, overlooking that no data can be sent during the CP. Here the CP takes 2/10 = 20%, and the rate drops by that much. The subcarrier spacing is 1/8 µs = 125 kHz, and since pilot and guard subcarriers carry no data either, there are fewer data subcarriers than FFT points.

ofdm-mimo-019.question: In a MIMO system with four transmit and four receive antennas, the channel matrix follows independent Rayleigh fading, and the transmitter, without channel knowledge, splits its power equally among the antennas. In the high-SNR region, about how much does the average capacity increase when the SNR is raised by 3 dB?
choices: About 1 b/s/Hz
About 16 b/s/Hz
About 4 b/s/Hz
ofdm-mimo-019.explanation: At high SNR, MIMO capacity grows as C ≈ min(Nt, Nr)·log₂(SNR) + constant. Raising the SNR by 3 dB (a factor of 2) increases log₂ by 1, so each of the four parallel streams gains about 1 b/s/Hz, about 4 b/s/Hz in total. This slope, min(Nt, Nr), is called the multiplexing gain (degrees of freedom). About 1 b/s/Hz is the increase with one antenna at each end (SISO). About 16 b/s/Hz wrongly takes the product of the antenna counts, Nt × Nr, as the slope; the product is what governs the maximum diversity order (the slope of the error rate). In strongly correlated channels the effective rank drops and this slope becomes smaller as well.

ofdm-mimo-020.question: In MIMO-OFDM with four transmit antennas, which correctly describes how pilots are sent so the receiver can estimate the channel from each transmit antenna?
choices: Each transmit antenna sends pilots that are mutually orthogonal in time, frequency, or code, so the four channels are estimated separately
If the four antennas send the same pilot on the same subcarrier at the same time, each channel can be found from the single summed value at the receiver
Pilots are sent for only one transmit antenna, and since the antennas are close together, the other three channels are taken to be the same value and reused
ofdm-mimo-020.explanation: What a receive antenna picks up is the sum of the signals from all transmit antennas, each through its own channel. If all antennas send the same pilot at the same time and frequency, only the sum of the channels can be found, and the four cannot be separated. So each transmit antenna's pilots are placed on different subcarriers or symbols (with the other antennas sending nothing there), or sent with orthogonal codes, and each channel is estimated separately. As a result, the resources used for pilots grow in proportion to the number of transmit antennas (or streams). Spatial multiplexing gain comes from the channels being different from one another, so taking them to be the same and reusing the estimate makes it impossible to separate the streams.
